title: evidence-ttl-slo-and-grace-periods-for-audit-events
summary: Working notes defining TTL tiers, SLOs, legal hold behavior, and operational recovery sequences for audit/evidence events. Emphasis on graceful retention enforcement, SIEM export fidelity, and RBAC v2 implications.
content:
Purpose
This doc captures operational guidance and pragmatic decisions for audit event retention (TTL) and SLOs across our stores (hot index, warm index, blob storage, SIEM export). It is an ops-focused cookbook: how we enforce retention, how we react to pipeline failures, and how RBAC v2 and evidence automation affect retention decisions.

High-level principles
- Preserve forensic integrity: events required for investigations or legal holds must not be dropped by automated TTLs.
- Cost-aware tiering: move older, low-access events to cheaper storage while keeping rehydration paths.
- Observable and reversible: retention actions must be logged, audited, and reversible when under legal hold.
- Minimize data divergence: SIEM exports should be as close to the source as practical; handle eventual consistency explicitly.

Retention tiers (recommended)
1) Hot index (0–90 days): full fidelity, sub-second query SLO for internal audits. Primary store for product+security SLOs.
2) Warm index (91–365 days): compressed index, no real-time ingestion guarantee; queries are slower (seconds).
3) Cold blob (1–7 years): gzipped/parquet blobs in object storage, indexed by minimal metadata (id, timestamp, event_type, tenant). Rehydrate to warm/hot on demand.
4) Archive/long-term (7+ years): legal-hold only (cold mirror, write-once). Access requires approved runbook and audit trail.

TTL and grace periods
- Default TTL per tenant: 365 days.
- Shorter TTLS may be applied to non-sensitive subsystems (eg analytics-only event streams): 90 days.
- Grace period on deletion: 72 hours between scheduled deletion job and irrevocable wipe to allow emergency holds.
- Legal hold overrides: when a hold is placed, disable scheduled expiry for all matching artifacts. Holds must be immutable (recorded with actor, timestamp, reason).

Enforcement mechanics
- Deletion jobs run nightly per shard/tenant. Stages: mark-for-deletion -> audit-log-entry -> soft-delete (move to quarantine bucket) -> final-delete after grace.
- Soft-delete is required to support fast recovery (restore from quarantine within 7 days).
- Final-delete is performed via lifecycle policy with a separate audit entry signed by system identity.
- For indices, we use index lifecycle policies to roll indices and shrink shards before snapshot + delete. For small tenants we group multiple tenants per index with tenant-tags.

SIEM export behavior and guarantees
- Export semantics: best-effort at-at-least-once delivery to SIEM sink. We cannot guarantee strict ordering during large backfills or replays.
- Retention mapping: events exported to SIEM must be preserved in vendor for a minimum of 90 days (contractual). If client requests longer SIEM retention, we flag via metadata and adjust export policy.
- Drift handling: if the SIEM sink confirms loss, we attempt re-export from cold blob within 30 days if available. After 30 days, rehydration is possible but may be missing intermediate state (eg KV caches).

RBAC v2 implications
- RBAC v2 introduces tenant-scoped deletion privileges. Only 'data-retention-admin' role can place/unplace legal holds and initiate final-delete.
- Deletion job service account must have a narrow ephemeral elevation path recorded in the audit log (who escalated, why, TTL).
- Access to rehydrate/archive artifacts is gated by 'forensics-read' and 'forensics-restore' roles; any restore action emits an evidence access event.

Backfill and reindex strategies
- Backfill triggers: schema changes, index optimization, SIEM re-exports, or corruption repair.
- Preferred path: reindex from cold blob snapshots to a staging cluster, run validation (checksum + sample queries), then swap aliases to avoid double-writing.
- For small reindexes (< 50M events) prefer live reindex; for larger sets use offline staging to avoid production impact.
- Throttling: use adaptive concurrency based on current CPU latency metrics; default = 10% of cluster capacity.

Failure modes and response checklist
1) Missed SIEM exports (partial)
   - Detect: export-lag alert > 2 hours or high retry rate.
   - Mitigation: escalate to on-call, run targeted re-export job for missing tenant/time-range, increase ephemeral throughput for export pipeline.
   - Postmortem action: capture root cause, add invariant check (sink ack vs internal checkpoint).
2) Index corruption or shard failure
   - Detect: index_health != green, checksum mismatch.
   - Mitigation: failover to replica, restore from snapshot of warm/cold tier if replica unavailable.
   - If snapshot older than required, initiate rehydrate from blob store and rebuild index.
3) Deletion job accidentally runs on wrong tenant
   - Detect: spike in deletion audit events, owner alert.
   - Mitigation: pause deletion pipeline immediately, mark impacted artifacts as quarantined, escalate legal/team leads. Attempt restore from quarantine (soft-delete buffer).
   - Postmortem: add dry-run validation step and tenant-safe-guard checkbox for next runs.
4) Legal hold misapplied or not cleared
   - Detect: investigators flag missing events or hold inventory mismatch.
   - Mitigation: if hold missing, search for soft-deleted artifacts and rehydrate; if wrongly applied, require approval to lift with two approvers.

Monitoring and SLOs
- Metrics to emit: retention_age_distribution, soft_delete_count, final_delete_count, quarantine_restores, siem_export_lag, rehydrate_success_rate, legal_hold_count.
- Key SLOs: 99.9% scheduled-deletions executed within 24h window; SIEM export lag < 5 minutes for hosted-tier, < 1 hour for dedicated-tier; rehydrate success rate > 95% for requests within 30 days.

Operational playbook snippets
- Emergency restore (short path): 1) Suspend deletion pipeline, 2) Search quarantine by tenant + timeframe, 3) Restore artifacts to warm index staging, 4) Run validation queries, 5) Promote to alias, 6) Record restore action in audit.
- SIEM reconciliation run: compare export checkpoints vs SIEM ack list, report missing segments, re-export missing ranges in time-sliced batches, mark completed in reconciliation ticket.

Cost and capacity notes
- Estimate: 1B events/year ~ 10 TB hot, 50 TB warm, 200 TB cold compressed. Adjust by event size and sampling rates.
- Encourage teams to reduce noise events (debug-level telemetry) and annotate events with retention-class tags to avoid storing high-cardinality ephemeral traces in hot tier.

Open questions and follow-ups
- Should the default tenant TTL be lowered to 180 days for non-security tenants to reduce cost? (tradeoff: reduces rehydrate window)
- How do we surface legal hold duration and approval metadata in the Console? Need product/console ticket.
- RBAC v2: define the exact permission set for the deletion job service account (SEC-1123).

Notes to self / TODOs
- Add sample queries for retention_age_distribution to shared dashboards.
- Draft compliance-ready phraseology for customer-facing retention policy doc.
- Schedule dry-run of deletion job in staging next quarter with failsafe canary.

References

- JIRA SEC-1123 (RBAC v2 deletion-perm work)
- infra repo: github.com/redwood/infra/audit-archives (scripts, snapshots)

End of notes.
